prompt: With hash(key) mod N, about what share of keys move when one of 10 nodes fails?
explanation: Going from mod 10 to mod 9 changes the result for about 90% of keys, since a key stays put only when both formulas happen to agree. (a) is what consistent hashing would move. (b) underestimates how badly mod N reshuffles. (d) Keys on the failed node must move at minimum.

scenario: A 4-node cache uses `hash(key) % 4`. You add a fifth node during peak and change to `% 5`. Database reads jump from 10,000/s to over 150,000/s and it falls over.

options.text: The new node was misconfigured and dropped every write sent to it
Changing to % 5 remapped about 80% of keys and emptied the cache
Only the new node's 20% share was cold, which overloaded the DB
The new node's slower hash function made every cache lookup time out

explanation: Changing N reassigns most keys: going from % 4 to % 5 moves about 80%, and every moved key is a miss, so the database is flooded. (a) A single faulty node would cost about 20% of keys, not a 15× jump. (c) describes what consistent hashing would have done; a 20% cold share wouldn't cause a 15× spike. (d) Hash cost is tiny and the same function runs everywhere.

prompt: On a consistent hashing ring, which node owns a key?

options.text: The node whose ID number is numerically closest
The first node clockwise from the key's position
The node at the key's position mod the node count
The node currently holding the fewest stored keys

explanation: Hash the key onto the ring and walk clockwise to the first node. (a) 'Closest' in either direction isn't the rule, and node IDs aren't ring positions. (c) brings back mod N, which is what the ring replaces. (d) Ownership is fixed by position, not by current load.

prompt: About what fraction of keys move when a node is added to N existing nodes?

options.text: None; existing keys stay where they are
About 1/(N+1) of the keys
About half, split with its neighbour
About N/(N+1), as with mod N

explanation: The new node takes only the arc between itself and its predecessor, about 1/(N+1) of the keys; nothing else moves. (a) is the lesson's misconception: some keys must move to the new node. (c) The new node takes part of one arc, not half the keyspace. (d) is the mod-N figure the ring avoids.

prompt: How is the owner of a key found efficiently?

options.text: Hash the key mod the node count
Binary search over sorted node positions
Broadcast the key and let its owner reply
Walk every node position in ring order

explanation: Keep node positions in a sorted array and binary search for the first one at or after the key's hash: O(log N). (a) is mod N, not the ring. (c) costs a network round to every node. (d) works but is O(N) per lookup.

prompt: What problem do virtual nodes solve?

options.text: One very popular key overloading the single node that owns it
Uneven arcs, and one neighbour absorbing a failed node's load
The ring's need to rehash every key when the node count changes
Slow lookups, since vnodes let you skip the sorted-position search

explanation: With only a few random positions, arcs are uneven, and when a node fails its single neighbour gets all its load. Many small arcs per node fix both. (a) Hot keys aren't fixed by vnodes; one key still lands on one node. (c) The ring already avoids rehashing everything. (d) Vnodes add positions, so the binary search is over more entries, not fewer.

prompt: How should you configure the cluster?
scenario: A cache cluster mixes 64 GB and 128 GB nodes. Each currently has 100 vnodes, so the small nodes fill up and evict long before the big ones.

options.text: Keep 100 vnodes each and let eviction even out the load
Give the 128 GB nodes about twice as many vnodes
Give the 64 GB nodes more vnodes so they get smaller arcs
Place the big nodes at fixed, evenly spaced ring positions

explanation: Vnode count acts as a weight, so each node's share of keys follows its capacity: twice the memory, about twice the vnodes. (a) Equal counts are what cause the imbalance. (c) More vnodes means more total arc, so this sends the small nodes even more keys. (d) Fixed positions don't change how many keys each node gets relative to its size.

prompt: Why didn't consistent hashing help, and what does?
scenario: Your consistent-hashed cache has 200 vnodes per node and an even key spread, but one node is at 100% CPU during a product launch. All its traffic is for one key: `product:launch-page`.

options.text: 200 vnodes is too few; raising it to 1,000 per node spreads the key
It balances keys, not traffic; cache the hot key locally or split it
The key's hash collides with another hot key; switch hash functions
That node has too few replicas; add more and read from any of them

explanation: Consistent hashing spreads keys, not requests: one hot key always lands on one node. Cache it locally in app servers or split it into several sub-keys. (a) More vnodes still place one key on one node. (c) A collision isn't the cause; all the traffic is genuinely for one key. (d) Replicas can help reads only if the client spreads reads to them, and that is a separate fix, not something adding replicas does by itself.

prompt: In Dynamo-style stores with R = 3, where are a key's replicas?

options.text: On the next 3 vnode positions clockwise, whichever nodes own them
On the next 3 distinct physical nodes clockwise from the key
On 3 nodes picked at random, recorded in a central lookup table
On the owner plus the 2 nodes directly counter-clockwise from it

explanation: Walk clockwise and take the next 3 distinct physical nodes (the preference list), skipping extra vnodes of nodes already chosen. (a) Consecutive vnodes can belong to the same machine, so two 'replicas' could share a node. (c) Dynamo avoids a central table; placement comes from the ring. (d) The direction is clockwise, matching how ownership is found.

prompt: Where is consistent hashing commonly used? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dynamo-style databases like Cassandra
Cache clients picking a memcached node
Load balancers wanting sticky backends
Hashing user passwords before storage

explanation: All of (a), (b) and (c) spread keys over a changing set of nodes. Password hashing (d) is a security hash, not a placement scheme; consistent hashing isn't itself a hash function.
